title: The Printing Press
objective: After this level you can explain how Gutenberg's press changed Europe after 1450.
summary: Around 1450 in Mainz, Gutenberg printed with reusable metal type. By 1500 Europe's few thousand manuscript books had become more than 9 million printed ones.

cards.headline: Before printing, Europe’s books numbered in the thousands. By 1500: millions.
cards.body: Remember Level 7’s monks, copying every book letter by letter? One workshop in Mainz changed the arithmetic. How?

cards.headline: Letters you can use again
cards.body: Johannes Gutenberg worked on his invention in Strasbourg and Mainz, and by about 1450 it was working well. The secret was movable type: single letters cast from a metal alloy that melted easily and cooled quickly into tough, reusable pieces. Set them in lines, print a page, then break them up and set the next. A scribe wrote every letter of every copy. Gutenberg’s letters worked like Scrabble tiles you could play again and again.

cards.headline: Borrowed from the wine press
cards.body: To press ink onto a page firmly and evenly, Gutenberg built a press, probably adapted from the ones used for wine, oil or paper. His showpiece, the 42-line Bible, came off it in Mainz around 1455, in a run of perhaps as many as 180 copies. About a quarter were printed on vellum, the same animal skin the monks of Level 7 wrote on. Old material, new machine.

cards.headline: From thousands to millions
cards.body: Before printing, Europe’s manuscript books could be counted in thousands. By 1500, after only 50 years of printing, there were more than 9 million. Why so fast? A printer ran off a whole edition at once, usually about 250 copies, and the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius printed 1,000. Remember that a monastery with 600 books had a large library? One print run could now outnumber it.
cards.callout: Before printing: thousands of books. By 1500: more than 9 million

mascot.line: This is Level 7’s scriptorium, overtaken: one print run could outnumber a whole library.

cards.headline: The printing press: explained
learned: Gutenberg printed with reusable metal type by about 1450
His press was adapted from wine or oil presses
The 42-line Bible came out in Mainz around 1455
By 1500 Europe had more than 9 million books

questions.prompt: What was the key idea behind Gutenberg’s printing in Mainz?

options.label: Carving each page as a single wooden block
options.rationale: His letters were separate pieces, reused page after page.

options.label: Reusable metal letters, reset for every page
Teams of scribes copying the same page at once
Stamping letters with hot wax seals
options.rationale: He cast letters from a metal alloy.

questions.explanation: Gutenberg cast single letters from a metal alloy; they could be set, printed and reset again and again.

questions.prompt: Why did printing multiply Europe’s books so quickly?

options.label: Printers used cheaper ink than scribes
options.rationale: Speed came from printing whole editions.

options.label: Kings ordered every town to open a press
options.rationale: No royal order is behind it.

options.label: Monasteries stopped copying books by hand
options.rationale: The press, not a ban on copying, did it.

options.label: One setting of type printed a whole edition

questions.explanation: A printer ran off an edition of about 250 copies, sometimes 1,000, in the time a scribe made one copy.

questions.prompt: A monastery with 600 books once had a large library. How did a single print run by Aldus Manutius compare?

options.label: It was far smaller, about 50 copies
It was about the same, 600 copies
At 1,000 copies, it outnumbered the whole library
It was ten times larger, 6,000 copies

questions.explanation: Aldus printed editions of 1,000: one run of one book outnumbered a large monastic library.
